newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian Church backs opposition but gains little.
newsitem.headline: Serbian Church backs opposition but gains little.

text.p: After 46 days of silence the Serbian Orthodox Church finally threw its weight behind opposition protests that have rocked Yugoslavia since November.

But analysts said the move came too late to regain the church the popularity it lost supporting the Serb cause in nationalist wars and would mean little to the pro-democracy movement protesting daily on the streets of Belgrade.
On Thursday church leaders condemned Socialist authorities for election fraud and said they were attempting to provoke a civil war in their desire to cling to power.
The authorities "pitted Serbia against the whole world and are now trying to get us to quarrel among each other only to stay in power," the church said in the statement.
The Serbian opposition launched mass protests after the authorities annulled November 17 local election results that showed the opposition had won 15 of Serbia's 18 largest towns, including Belgrade.
It was the church's first public stand on the crisis and appeared to come only after heavy prompting from leading opposition figure Vuk Draskovic.
"It is a big question whether the Church would have spoken even this late had not Vuk Draskovic taken them to task a few days ago," Milos Vasic of the independent Belgrade weekly Vreme, told Reuters.
Draskovic, a partner in the Zajedno opposition coalition, asked the Church at a recent rally in Belgrade "how many people more have to die before you take a stand."
Serbian Orthodox Church leader, Patriarch Pavle, early last month refused to bless a delegation of protesting Belgrade students.
He later reversed his position and last week blessed the students but "too late to diminish the bitter aftertaste of the snub," a senior analyst said.
The church lost much popularity for its strong support for the nationalist cause in wars in Bosnia and Croatia since 1991.
Its pro-war stance resulted in political marginalisation and a loss of credibility among the moderate majority in Serbia that it will find hard to recover, diplomats and analysts say.

Although it never liked Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, a former communist official with little time for the ecclesiastical hierarchy, the Church backed him strongly when he fostered their expansionist dreams.
But it grew disgruntled when Milosevic dropped his support for Serbs in rebel-held Croatia and in Bosnia.
But the opposition is not rushing to embrace the church for its now open criticism of Milosevic's socialist authorities.
Its overall reputation is poor. Priests were quick to flee fighting in the war and not one priest was killed, a fact that did not go unnoticed among refugees and citizens.

The church never played a major role in a society where communism has deep roots, unlike in other East European countries where the ideology was imposed by the former Soviet Union and clergy led the fight for democracy.
The Zajedno coalition, which comprises a wide spectrum of political forces from rightist royalists to centrist democrats, has yet to woo organised labour.
"The Church will not have major influence on the workers' decision to abstain or join the demonstrations," one senior western analyst said.
